about: LedgerMath runs small benchmarks on real AWS machines several times a day and keeps every execution as a Run. A Series is the Runs of one benchmark, parameter set, build, instance type and Availability Zone ID; a versioned Method turns its Runs into a Derivation. This is version 1 of the data API: static JSON files cut from the Derivations and the daily price files, each kind with a JSON schema. A Series' file holds each Method's summary and its newest Runs; every Run's point is in the file of the month it started in, and months says when such a file changes.
versioning: Version 1 only ever gains fields. A field, once in a v1 file, keeps its name, its type and its meaning, and a reader ignores any field it does not know: that is why no object in the schemas index, series-list, benchmark, series and series-month forbids members it does not list. A new Method, or a new version of one, is a new key beside the old ones. A change that would break a reader is published as v2, beside v1. The price files are the exception: each is the day's price file as LedgerMath keeps it, byte for byte, and follows its own schema, ledgermath.prices/1, whose root and LedgerMath's own objects are closed (AWS's objects within it are open).
figures: Every number is exactly as the Methods' Derivations hold it: nothing is rounded, and nothing is computed that the Derivations do not hold, apart from counts of a Series' Runs (in all, in a month, in a group, counted and not) and of the boots they were made on, the start times of its oldest and newest Run (in all, in a month, in a group), taken from its points, the counts of each benchmark's Series and of their Runs and the start of their newest Run, and how many Series are in no benchmark's list (benchmarks), each month file's sha256 and size in bytes, and the counts of each of the newest rounds of boots (recent_rounds), taken from the boot summaries and the points. A duration is in nanoseconds of the Run's clock unless its field's name says otherwise; a moment is a UTC time, to the nanosecond, as the Run records it.
months: Each Series is split by month: every Run's point is in the file of the month the Run started in (UTC, by the Run's start), with series v1's entry for each pair of consecutive Runs under the month of the later Run, and the Series' file lists its months. For a given layout (the layout of v1/index.json), a month file's bytes change only when (a) a Run that started in that month is added, (b) a boot summary that was missing arrives, (c) a Run arrives late, having started before a Run of the Series already in the files, in that month or an earlier one, or (d) a Method first applies to the Series; otherwise they do not change. These four are the only causes for a given layout: layout increases when LedgerMath changes how the files are written, and only then may a file's bytes change without one of them. A past month is therefore not immutable: each entry of the Series file's months gives its month file's sha256 and size in bytes, so a reader holding a copy can tell whether it is current, and fetches the file again only when the sha256 differs. A Series file and a month file fetched together can still be from different updates of the files: a cache may hold one of them from before the other changed, and an update that stopped halfway leaves them so until the next one. So a reader checks the sha256 of every month file it fetches against the one its Series file lists; on a mismatch, it fetches the Series file again, then the month file, and compares again; while they still differ, it uses neither, and tries again later. What each cause changes: (a) the month gains the Run's point, its pair entry and its count and span; (b) the point's boot_summary turns from null into the summary's address, and nothing else; (c) as (a), and in that month and every later one the points after the late Run may change only what depends on earlier Runs: their group, and requests v1's through and group_through_as_of_run (through's counts rise by exactly what the late Runs it pools add, and not at all when none of them is counted), and the pair entry of the Run right after it then comes from the late Run; (d) the Method's block appears, under its key, in every month file of the Series.

recent_rounds.about: A round is the boots that belong together in time, worked out from the boot summaries alone, so the same boot summaries always give the same rounds: the boots in order of their start, a boot starting a new round when it started more than 40 minutes after the boot before it. rounds holds the newest 8 rounds, newest first. LedgerMath boots each of its machine types a few minutes apart, several times a day, each boot a fresh machine that leaves a Run for each execution it runs: a round is normally one of those times, with a boot for each machine type booted then, and a boot started by hand away from them is a round of its own. Each round gives when its first boot started, how many boots it holds and their instance types, how many Runs they left (the Runs their summaries list), how many of those are failed and how many are in no Series, how many builds failed and how many executions were not run, in all and by boot, with the address of each boot's summary, which lists each of them. A Run is failed when it is not counted by Method requests v1, for a Run of a Series that Method derives (a Series of requests), or by Method series v1, for a Run of any other Series: so a Run of requests that exited 4, a request having failed, is failed only when requests v1 does not count it, though series v1 does not count it either way, and the failed Runs are the points with counted false in their Series' month files, under that Method, as its failed_runs in each Series' file counts them. A Run in no Series has no Run file in the evidence, or one no Method could read. Each round lists its first 12 boots by start, with their instance types, and its figures count every boot. left_out counts every file of the evidence's boot summaries that is in no round, and lists the newest 8 by path, each with its path, its address when the API serves it, and why. A path is written with each byte of its name that is not printable ASCII, and each %, double quote and backslash, as % and two hex digits; one longer than 120 characters is cut to its first 101, then ..., then the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the whole. A file is in no round when the API does not serve its address (decided by its name alone, the file unread), when it cannot be read, lacks what a round needs (an instance type of 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, hyphens or underscores among it) or is not at the path its own contents give, every summary of a boot but the one that started first, one listing a Run whose point is of another boot, and each of two listing one Run. A Run's point links its boot's summary: the one of its boot that started first, of those at the path their own contents give that a round can read. A boot left out is in no round, and its path gives the day it started: a round shown within 40 minutes of it may be missing that boot. Any round shown may change at a later update, not only the newest: a boot is in a round once its summary is in the evidence, which the boot writes when it ends and which may arrive later still. A summary that arrives late joins the round its start falls within, which then gains a boot and its figures, may start earlier, and becomes one round with the round before or after it when the boot started within 40 minutes of both, so that a round further back moves into the list or out of it. A summary that arrives in conflict with one already read (naming its boot, or listing one of its Runs) takes that boot out of its round, which may split the round in two. A Run file that arrives late moves its Run from in no Series to counted or failed. And the list moves on as new rounds arrive, the oldest leaving it.

series.about: The list of every Series (url) gives one row per Series, and each benchmark's list (benchmarks) that benchmark's rows; a row gives the Series' identity, a summary of each Method's Derivation of it and the address of its file (url). A Series' id is 12 lower-case hex digits, the first of the sha256 of its key (benchmark, params, build, instance type, zone ID) as canonical JSON: a row gives it (id), as do the Series' file and a citation of the Series. A reader who holds an id and nothing else gets the Series' file at series_file_url_template, {id} replaced by the id. A Series' file gives the address of each of its month files, so no other address need be built.

benchmarks.about: Each benchmark's Series are listed in a file of their own, v1/benchmarks/<benchmark>.json: rows of the list of every Series, v1/series.json, under a head like the list's (count, newest_run_started_at) with the benchmark's name and left_out; in files of one update, each row is the same, byte for byte, in the same order. The table of contents, a benchmark's list, the list of every Series and a Series' file are each whole, but fetched together they can be of different updates of the files: an update writes them one after another, a cache may hold one of them from before another changed, and an update that stopped part way leaves them so until the next one. Their counts and rows can then differ: one may hold a Series, or count a Run, that another does not. So a reader takes each file as true of its own update; where two of them differ, it fetches them again later, and they agree once both are of one update. Every benchmark whose name is 1 to 64 characters, a lower-case letter, then lower-case letters, digits and underscores, has its list, always; its address is benchmark_file_url_template with {benchmark} replaced by the name, which every row and every Series' file gives (benchmark). The Series of a benchmark named otherwise are in v1/series.json alone. A list holds, of its benchmark's Series whose rows take at most 16384 bytes written as JSON with no white space, in its order, as many as fit in 250000 bytes, each row counted as those bytes and 6 more; the first that does not fit and every one after it are left out, and the list counts them (left_out). So a Series its benchmark's list holds is two requests from this file: the list, then the Series' file at its row's url; one in no list is found through v1/series.json. Every Series, listed or not, has its own file. Each entry of list gives a benchmark's name, its list's address, how many Series the list holds (series), how many Runs they hold (runs) and when the newest of them started (newest_run_started_at): in name order, as many as fit in 16000 bytes, each counted the same way; count says how many benchmarks have a list, unlisted how many of them list does not name, and left_out how many Series are in no benchmark's list, for any of these reasons. So what the Runs hold cannot make this file or a benchmark's list too large to publish.

schemas.name: events
schemas.describes: one line of a Run's stdout: the blob at blobs/sha256/<hex> that the Run file's stdout names

evidence.about: The evidence is served under the same address as the API: each point links its Run file (evidence), at runs/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<id>.json, and its boot's summary (boot_summary), at boots/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<boot>.json. A Run file names its binary, streams and dumps by hash, sha256:<hex>; each is a blob at blob_url_template with {hex} replaced by the 64 hex digits. The blob its stdout names is what the binary printed, one event a line; the schema events, in schemas, gives the shape each line must have for a Method to count the Run.
